claim: Efficient transportation is crucial for urban mobility, cell function and the survival of animal groups.
source: Efficient transportation is crucial for urban mobility, cell function and the survival of animal groups.
evidence: This is a general statement drawing from established scientific understanding about the importance of transportation in various systems.

claim: Ants avoid the formation of traffic jams at high density despite their behavioral simplicity.
source: Here, we show that ants, despite their behavioral simplicity, have managed the tour de force of avoiding the formation of traffic jams at high density.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing flow remains constant at high densities.

claim: At low densities there is a clear linear relationship between ant density and the flow.
source: At low densities there is a clear linear relationship between ant density and the flow, while at large density, the flow remains constant and no congestion occurs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and the two-phase flow model.

claim: At large density, the flow remains constant and no congestion occurs.
source: At low densities there is a clear linear relationship between ant density and the flow, while at large density, the flow remains constant and no congestion occurs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 demonstrating a plateau in flow at high densities.

claim: Ants adjust their speed at large densities.
source: From a microscopic perspective, the individual tracking of ants under varying densities revealed that ants adjust their speed and avoid time consuming interactions at large densities.
evidence: This is supported by individual tracking data showing speed changes with density (Figure 6A).

claim: Ants avoid time consuming interactions at large densities.
source: From a microscopic perspective, the individual tracking of ants under varying densities revealed that ants adjust their speed and avoid time consuming interactions at large densities.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that contact time remains short and flow remains constant despite high density.

claim: Many organisms take part in flow-like collective movements.
source: Many organisms such as herds of migrating wildebeests, swarms of insects and bacteria, starling flocks, fish shoals or pedestrian crowds take part in flow-like collective movements (Ball, 2004; Berdahl et al., 2013; Berdahl et al., 2018; Buhl et al., 2006; Chowdhury et al., 2005; Fourcassié et al., 2010; Giardina, 2008; John et al., 2009; Moussaïd et al., 2011; Sumpter, 2010; Vicsek and Zafeiris, 2012; Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Along with humans, ants are one of the rare animals in which collective movements are bidirectional.
source: Along with humans (Helbing et al., 2005; Moussaïd et al., 2011), ants are one of the rare animals in which collective movements are bidirectional.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on human and ant traffic.

claim: Ants are central-place foragers, which entails a succession of journeys between their nest and their foraging site.
source: Ants are central-place foragers, which entails a succession of journeys between their nest and their foraging site.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ant foraging behavior.

claim: When exploiting large food sources, many ant species lay chemical trails along which individuals commute back and forth.
source: When exploiting large food sources, many species lay chemical trails along which individuals commute back and forth (Czaczkes et al., 2015; Gordon, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on ant trail-laying behavior.

claim: The flow of individuals on ant trails can reach several hundred ants per minute.
source: The flow of individuals on these trails can reach several hundred ants per minute (Couzin and Franks, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Ants seem to fare better than humans when it comes to traffic management.
source: Yet, ants seem to fare better than us when it comes to traffic management (Burd et al., 2002; Dussutour et al., 2004; Fourcassié et al., 2010; Hönicke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on ant traffic.

claim: There is a lack of direct experimental evidence showing that ants do not get stuck in traffic jam at high density.
source: However, we lack direct experimental evidence showing that ants do not get stuck in traffic jam at high density (Burd et al., 2002; Hönicke et al., 2015; John et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations indicating gaps in previous research.

claim: The Greenshields function was the first speed-density relation function used to analyze data recorded for vehicular traffic in the field.
source: The Greenshields function (Greenshields et al., 1935) was the first speed-density relation function used to analyze data recorded for vehicular traffic in the field.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and described in Figure 1A.

claim: The Greenshields function assumes a linear relationship between v and k leading to a parabolic shape relation between q and k.
source: This function assumes a linear relationship between v and k leading to a parabolic shape relation between q and k.
evidence: This is a description of the mathematical properties of the Greenshields function shown in Figure 1A.

claim: A total of 170 experiments were performed.
source: A total of 170 experiments were performed.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: In average 94% of the ants fed once at the food source.
source: In average 94% of the ants fed once at the food source.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bridge width does not affect ant speed when ants are traveling alone.
source: Second, we controlled that the bridge width itself did not affect ant speed. In absence of interactions and when ants were traveling alone, their speed was similar regardless of the bridge width (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The flow q increased with the density k to a certain point and then it remained constant.
source: The flow q increased with the density k to a certain point and then it remained constant.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: All the statistical models performed similarly well but failed at predicting the data at intermediate and large densities.
source: All the statistical models performed similarly well but failed at predicting the data at intermediate and large densities.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of model fits shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The two-phase statistical model was selected based on model selection analysis using Akaike weights.
source: Then, we conducted a model selection analysis using Akaike weights to assign conditional probabilities to all statistical models. Thanks to our large dataset, the result was unequivocal: the two-phase statistical model was selected (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2C and supplementary materials.

claim: No clear evidence of spatiotemporal organization was observed in ant traffic at high density.
source: However, in our experiments, no clear evidence of such organizations was observed.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations described in the text and shown in Figure 3.

claim: When ant density reached a critical threshold, inbound and outbound flows became intermingled temporally.
source: In contrast, when ant density reached a critical threshold, inbound and outbound flows became intermingled temporally (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and spatially (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: When ant density reached a critical threshold, inbound and outbound flows became intermingled spatially.
source: In contrast, when ant density reached a critical threshold, inbound and outbound flows became intermingled temporally (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and spatially (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Video 1 and Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and videos.

claim: The relationship between density k and flow q was only marginally influenced by the degree of asymmetry in the flows.
source: In addition, contrary to pedestrian traffic (Helbing et al., 2005; Moussaïd et al., 2011), the relationship between density k and flow q was only marginally influenced by the degree of asymmetry in the flows (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: As density k grew, the number of contacts C increased linearly (C = 0.61 k).
source: As density k grew, the number of contacts C increased linearly (C = 0. 61 k Figure 4A) that is the larger the density, the higher the number of contacts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A with a linear regression.

claim: Each contact slowed down the ants with a linear effect on traveling time T (T = T0 + C · ∆T with T0 = 0.95 s and ∆T = 0.24 s).
source: We observed a linear effect of the number of contacts C on traveling time T, that is each contact slowed down the ants. (T = T0 + C · ∆T with T0 = 0.95 s and ∆T = 0.24 s, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B with a linear regression.

claim: T0 can be interpreted as the traveling time to cross the bridge without contacts (free flow traveling time).
source: T0 can be interpreted as the traveling time to cross the bridge without contacts (free flow traveling time), whereas ∆T is the time lost per contact.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the parameter T0 from the linear regression model.

claim: ∆T is the time lost per contact.
source: T0 can be interpreted as the traveling time to cross the bridge without contacts (free flow traveling time), whereas ∆T is the time lost per contact.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the parameter ∆T from the linear regression model.

claim: For a given number of contacts C, ants moved faster on the bridge at intermediate density k (i.e. k ≈ 5).
source: As expected, traveling time T increased with the number of contacts C, but the key information is that density k actually made traveling time T decay initially (up to k ≈ 5). For a given number of contacts C, ants moved faster on the bridge at intermediate density k (i.e. k ≈ 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Free flow speed vf is first increasing with density k up to k≈5 ants.cm−2 and then decays back to its initial value.
source: vf is first increasing with density k up to k≈5 ants.cm−2 and then decays back to its initial value.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The positive effect of density on speed might be explained by a pheromone effect.
source: This phenomenon might be explained by a pheromone effect.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed positive effect of density on speed.

claim: Argentine ants deposit pheromones both when leaving and when returning to the nest and travel faster on a well-marked trail.
source: It is well known that Argentine ants deposit pheromones both when leaving and when returning to the nest and travel faster on a well-marked trail (Deneubourg et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The plateau reached for flow was q ≈ 10 ants.cm−1.s−1.
source: The plateau reached was q ≈ 10 ants.cm−1.s−1.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: When k < 5 ant.cm−2 ants moved faster, which positively impacted the flow q.
source: Thus, even though increasing density k generated more contacts impacting negatively the flow q through their effect on traveling time T, when k < 5 ant.cm−2 ants moved faster, which positively impacted the flow q.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined analysis of speed and contact data.

claim: For k > 8 ants.cm−2, despite the crowdedness of the trail, ants maintained a constant flow q.
source: For k > 8 ants.cm−2, despite the crowdedness of the trail, ants maintained a constant flow q.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 6.

claim: The number of contacts increased only linearly with the density according to Figure 4A.
source: Given that the unoccupied portion of the bridge decayed with the density, it is remarkable that the number of contacts increased only linearly with the density according to Figure 4A (or one could argue even sub-linearly for k > 10 ants.cm−2).
evidence: This is based on the linear relationship shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Ants restrained themselves from leaving the nest to prevent overcrowding as k never exceeded 18 ant.cm−2.
source: Interestingly, we also observed that ants restrained themselves from leaving the nest to prevent overcrowding as k never exceeded 18 ant.cm−2 even though we increased colony size and reduced bridge width (number of ants entering the bridge for the largest colonies ± CI95: 2.69 ± 0.04, 4.34 ± 0.03 and 5.05 ± 0.03 ants.sec−1 for the 5, 10 and 20 mm bridges).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations across different colony sizes and bridge widths.

claim: U-turns were seldom once the ants were traveling on the bridge (probability of turning back once on the bridge = 0.01).
source: Furthermore, U-turns were seldom once the ants were traveling on the bridge (probability of turning back once on the bridge = 0.01).
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations.

claim: In pedestrian and car traffic, at occupancy levels above 0.4 the flow starts to decline.
source: In pedestrian and car traffic (Banks, 1999; Helbing et al., 2005), at occupancy levels above 0.4 the flow starts to decline, while in ants, the flow showed no sign of declining even when occupancy reached 0.8.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on human traffic.

claim: In ants, the flow showed no sign of declining even when occupancy reached 0.8.
source: In pedestrian and car traffic (Banks, 1999; Helbing et al., 2005), at occupancy levels above 0.4 the flow starts to decline, while in ants, the flow showed no sign of declining even when occupancy reached 0.8.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the current study.

claim: Ants seem to be immune to traffic congestion.
source: Here, by investigating traffic dynamics on a large range of densities, we demonstrated that ants seem to be immune to traffic congestion.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by all experimental data showing constant flow at high densities.

claim: In ants, traffic is governed by positive feed-backs (trail following and reinforcement).
source: In contrast, in ants, traffic is governed by positive feed-backs (trail following and reinforcement) and interactions which are time consuming but often beneficial for the colony as they promotes information transfer (Bouchebti et al., 2015; Burd and Aranwela, 2003; Farji-Brener et al., 2010; Fourcassié et al., 2010; Gordon, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on ant behavior.

claim: Interactions in ants are time consuming but often beneficial for the colony as they promote information transfer.
source: In contrast, in ants, traffic is governed by positive feed-backs (trail following and reinforcement) and interactions which are time consuming but often beneficial for the colony as they promotes information transfer (Bouchebti et al., 2015; Burd and Aranwela, 2003; Farji-Brener et al., 2010; Fourcassié et al., 2010; Gordon, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Time spent interacting with other ants has strong consequences on traffic dynamics.
source: Nonetheless, time spent interacting with other ants has strong consequences on traffic dynamics (Gravish et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Short interaction time allows a smooth traffic over a wide range of densities whereas long interaction time promotes rapid slowing of traffic.
source: Short interaction time allows a smooth traffic over a wide range of densities whereas long interaction time promotes rapid slowing of traffic (Gravish et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In fire ants, Gravish et al. (2015) found that interaction time was relatively short (0.45 s).
source: In fire ants, Gravish et al. (2015) found that interaction time was relatively short (0.45 s) and that the flow was relatively unaffected by density up to a certain critical value beyond which they observed the formation of traffic jams (Gravish et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Argentine ants have an interaction time approximately twice shorter than fire ants.
source: Here, we found that Argentine ants have an interaction time approximately twice shorter than fire ants, which could explain why we observed a smooth and efficient mixing of opposite flows over a broader range of densities.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the interaction time data (0.24 s from Figure 4B) with fire ant data (0.45 s) from Gravish et al.

claim: When density on the trail increases, ants seemed to be able to assess crowding locally, and adjusted their speed accordingly to avoid any interruption of traffic flow.
source: The exact nature of the mechanisms used by Argentine ants to keep the traffic flowing in this study remains elusive, yet when density on the trail increases, ants seemed to be able to assess crowding locally, and adjusted their speed accordingly to avoid any interruption of traffic flow.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed speed adjustments with density shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ants restrained themselves from entering a crowded path and ensured that the capacity of the bridge was never exceeded.
source: Moreover, ants restrained themselves from entering a crowded path and ensured that the capacity of the bridge was never exceeded that is the maximum value of the flow allowed by the bridge width.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that density never exceeded 18 ant.cm−2.

claim: Traffic regulation on trails ultimately allows Argentine ants to maintain a high rate of food return to the nest.
source: Traffic regulation on trails ultimately allows Argentine ants to maintain a high rate of food return to the nest, an essential asset in the context of food competition occurring in natural environments.
evidence: This is an inference about the adaptive significance of the observed traffic regulation.

claim: In fire ants, behaviors such as 'individual idleness and retreating' at overcrowded digging sites supports an optimal accessibility of space facilitating excavation during nest construction.
source: For instance, in the nest-building context, behaviors such as 'individual idleness and retreating' at overcrowded digging sites supports an optimal accessibility of space facilitating excavation during nest construction in fire ants (Aguilar et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Carpenter ants placed under threat and forced to escape through a narrow door distribute themselves uniformly over the space available instead of rushing toward the door.
source: Similarly, carpenter ants placed under threat and forced to escape through a narrow door distribute themselves uniformly over the space available instead of rushing toward the door and trampling on others (Parisi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Carpenter ants avoid clogging and evacuate efficiently, contrary to humans.
source: As a result, contrary to humans (Helbing et al., 2000), they avoid clogging and evacuate efficiently (Parisi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In garden ants, the interplay between trail following behavior and collisions allows ants to cope with bottleneck situations.
source: Lastly, in garden ants, the interplay between trail following behavior and collisions allows ants to cope with bottleneck situations (Dussutour et al., 2006; Dussutour et al., 2005; Dussutour et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Ants behaved as a self-organized biological adaptive system.
source: Overall, our results extend previous research on ant traffic organization (Aguilar et al., 2018; Burd et al., 2002; Fourcassié et al., 2010; Gravish et al., 2015; Hönicke et al., 2015; John et al., 2009) and show that ant prevented traffic jams from occurring and behaved as a self-organized biological adaptive system (Camazine et al., 2003; Hemelrijk, 2005).
evidence: This is a conclusion supported by the experimental data and citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: Similar phenomena of self-regulation ought to be found in other complex systems such as migrating animals, cell machinery, swarm of robots and data traffic.
source: Similar phenomena of self-regulation ought to be found in other complex systems such as migrating animals (Buhl et al., 2006), cell machinery (Leduc et al., 2012), swarm of robots (Aguilar et al., 2018) and data traffic (Valverde and Solé, 2004) and could provide inspiration in all disciplines, ranging from molecular biology to automotive engineering.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications, supported by citations.

claim: The Argentine ant Linepithema humile is a major pest around the world.
source: We used the European supercolony of Argentine ants Linepithema humile, which is a major pest around the world and the largest recorded society of multicellular organisms (Giraud et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The Argentine ant is the largest recorded society of multicellular organisms.
source: We used the European supercolony of Argentine ants Linepithema humile, which is a major pest around the world and the largest recorded society of multicellular organisms (Giraud et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Argentine ants use mass recruitment through pheromone trails to exploit abundant food sources.
source: We used the Argentine ant Linepithema humile, an invasive species that uses mass recruitment through pheromone trails to exploit abundant food sources.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Argentine ant foraging behavior.

claim: Argentine ants have multiple queens and form supercolonies.
source: Argentine ants have multiple queens and form supercolonies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Argentine ant social structure.

claim: Established Argentine ant supercolonies can contain up to 108 workers.
source: Established supercolonies can contain up to 108 workers (Giraud et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Argentine ants are monomorphic (2.5 mm long).
source: These ants are monomorphic (2.5 mm long).
evidence: This is a factual description of the study organism.

claim: The experimental colonies were starved for five days before each experiment.
source: Before each experiment, the experimental colonies were starved for five days, and the experiment started when the ants were given access to a food source placed on a platform (120 × 120 mm for small colonies - up to 3200, or 230 × 230 mm for the larger colonies) at the other end of a plastic bridge.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental protocol.

claim: The total length of the bridge was 170 mm.
source: The total length of the bridge was 170 mm and the bridge width was either 5 mm (narrow bridge), 10 mm (medium bridge) or 20 mm (large bridge).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: The food consisted of a 1M sucrose solution.
source: The food consisted of a 1M sucrose solution contained in small grooves (100 mm long for small colonies and 185 mm for large colonies) carved in a block of Plexiglas.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: The number of replicates for each bridge width and each colony size ranged between 4 and 10.
source: The number of replicates for each bridge width and each colony size ranged between 4 and 10 leading to a total of 170 experiments.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Ants seldom climbed on top of each other that is the flow remained two-dimensional in all experiments.
source: Ants seldom climbed on top of each other that is the flow remained two-dimensional in all experiments.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Ants covered on average 3.5 mm2 excluding legs and antennae and 4.4 mm2 with legs and antennae.
source: Ants covered on average 3.5 mm2 excluding legs and antennae and 4.4 mm2 with legs and antennae.
evidence: This is a measurement from the experiments.

claim: Automatic analysis had a slight tendency to underestimate densities but only when density was higher than six ant.cm−2 (difference between manual and automatic −0.36 ant.cm−2+ /- IC95 0.02).
source: We found a good agreement although automatic analysis had a slight tendency to underestimate densities but only when density was higher than six ant.cm−2 (difference between manual and automatic −0.36 ant.cm−2+ /- IC95 0.02).
evidence: This is a validation of the measurement method.

claim: A physical contact lasted between 0.1 and 3.2·s (mean ± SD 0.18 ± 0.14 s).
source: A physical contact lasted between 0.1 and 3.2·s (mean ± SD 0.18 ± 0.14 s).
evidence: This is a measurement from the experiments.

claim: The flow q increases with the density k from zero to a maximum value and then decays until it goes back to zero at the so-called maximum jam density kj in typical traffic systems.
source: First, the flow q increases with the density k from zero to a maximum value and then decays until it goes back to zero at the so-called maximum jam density kj.
evidence: This is a description of typical traffic flow patterns from traffic engineering literature, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The speed is maximum when an individual is traveling alone (free flow speed vf) in typical traffic systems.
source: Second, the speed is maximum when an individual is traveling alone (free flow speed vf) and decreases with the density k.
evidence: This is a description of typical traffic flow patterns from traffic engineering literature.

claim: The speed becomes zero and individuals stop at jam density that is v(kj)=0 in typical traffic systems.
source: The speed becomes zero and individuals stop at jam density that is v(kj)=0 (Nagatani, 2002; Treiber et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to traffic engineering literature.

claim: In leaf-cutting ants, speed decreases when density increases.
source: In leaf-cutting ants (Burd et al., 2002) and fire ants (Gravish et al., 2015) speed decreases when density increases while for wood ants (Hönicke et al., 2015) and mass raiding ants (John et al., 2009) the speed remains constant when density increases.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In fire ants, speed decreases when density increases.
source: In leaf-cutting ants (Burd et al., 2002) and fire ants (Gravish et al., 2015) speed decreases when density increases while for wood ants (Hönicke et al., 2015) and mass raiding ants (John et al., 2009) the speed remains constant when density increases.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: For wood ants, the speed remains constant when density increases.
source: In leaf-cutting ants (Burd et al., 2002) and fire ants (Gravish et al., 2015) speed decreases when density increases while for wood ants (Hönicke et al., 2015) and mass raiding ants (John et al., 2009) the speed remains constant when density increases.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: For mass raiding ants, the speed remains constant when density increases.
source: In leaf-cutting ants (Burd et al., 2002) and fire ants (Gravish et al., 2015) speed decreases when density increases while for wood ants (Hönicke et al., 2015) and mass raiding ants (John et al., 2009) the speed remains constant when density increases.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The range of densities tested was large enough to observe traffic jams only in the study conducted with fire ants traveling in tunnels.
source: However, the range of densities tested was large enough to observe traffic jams only in the study conducted with fire ants traveling in tunnels (Gravish et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The highest densities recorded in leaf-cutting ants, wood ants and mass raiding ants were not sufficiently high to generate a traffic jam.
source: The highest densities as well as the estimated occupancy (fraction of area covered by ants), recorded in leaf-cutting ants (Burd et al., 2002), wood ants (Hönicke et al., 2015) and mass raiding ants (John et al., 2009) were relatively low: 0.8 ants.cm−2 (occupancy 0.20), 0.6 ants.cm−2 (0.13) and 0.3 ants.cm−2 (0.10) and not sufficiently high to generate a traffic jam as ants never exceeded the capacity of the trail, that is the maximum value of the flow allowed by the trail width.
evidence: This is based on analysis of data from cited previous research.

claim: The study succeeded in generating large variations of density (from 0 to 18 ants.cm−2) and occupancy (from 0 to 0.8).
source: We succeeded in generating large variations of density (from 0 to 18 ants.cm−2) and occupancy (from 0 to 0.8).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental achievement.

claim: The study conducted 612,000 flow/density (non-independent) observations pairs.
source: The flow q and the density k were recorded on each experiment every second for one hour giving us 612,000 flow/density (non-independent) observations pairs.
evidence: This is a description of the data collected.

claim: Ant traffic is best described by a two-phase flow function at the macroscopic level.
source: At the macroscopic level, we demonstrated that ant traffic is best described by a two-phase flow function.
evidence: This is the main finding supported by model selection analysis.
